name: Adna
title: Priest from the family of Pashhur and head of the priestly house of the Harim clan in the time of Joiakim
summary: Adna was a priest in Judah in the period after the Babylonian exile, when the rebuilding of the temple institution and religious renewal stood at the center of the people's life. In the book of Ezra he is listed among the priests of the family of Pashhur who had married women from foreign peoples, and who by Ezra's reform efforts committed themselves to dissolving these marriages in order to protect Israel's worship of God from syncretistic influence (Ezra 10:22). In the book of Nehemiah the name Adna appears as head of the priestly house of the family of Harim under the high priest Joiakim (Neh 12:15), a role that places him in a leading position within the temple organization. Whether these two references refer to one and the same person or to two different men with the same name is debated among scholars – the connection to different family lines (Pashhur and Harim) makes it likely that they are two different priests. In any case, both mentions shed light on the decisive function of the priesthood in the rebuilding of Jewish religious and social life after the exile.

keyEvents.title: Listed among priests with foreign wives
keyEvents.description: Adna from the family of Pashhur was identified as one of the priests who had married women from foreign nations. This was considered a serious violation of the Torah's provisions to protect Israel's worship from foreign religious influence.

keyEvents.title: The priests' commitment to send away foreign wives
keyEvents.description: In connection with Ezra's reform movement, the priests who had married foreign women committed themselves to separate from them in order to preserve the holiness of the people. Adna and the other priests mentioned in the list in Ezra 10:22 were part of this collective commitment, where giving one's hand on a pledge served as a covenantal sign of sincere repentance.

keyEvents.title: Head of the priestly house of the Harim clan in the time of Joiakim
keyEvents.description: In the book of Nehemiah, Adna is mentioned as head of the priestly house of the Harim clan during the high priesthood of Joiakim. This testifies to his prominent position in the temple organization in post-exilic Jerusalem.

versions.summary: Adna was a priest from the family of Pashhur who lived in the period after the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned in the book of Ezra as one of the priests who had taken foreign wives and who committed himself to send them away in accordance with Ezra's reforms. The name Adna also appears in the book of Nehemiah as a priest in the time of Joiakim.
versions.title: Priest who left his foreign wife
versions.reason: [major] Adna from the lineage of Pashhur is mentioned in Ezra 10:30, but this verse concerns the sons of Pahath-Moab, not the lineage of Pashhur. Adna from the lineage of Pashhur appears in Ezra 10:39. Verse 30 mentions other names. It is important to distinguish between the two occurrences of Adna in Ezra 10.; [major] Ezra 10:19 specifically describes priests from the lineage of Jeshua and his brothers who pledged to send away their foreign wives. This verse does not directly concern Adna, but rather gives a general description of the pledge. The personal connection to Adna is imprecise.; [major] Nehemiah 12:1-7 lists priests who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, a generation before Adna. Adna himself is first mentioned in Neh 12:15 as a head during the time of Joiakim. The reference to Neh 12:1-7 is not directly relevant to Adna and may mislead the reader.; [minor] The summary should clarify that there may be two different individuals named Adna: one in Ezra 10 (among priests with foreign wives) and one in Nehemiah 12 (head of the priestly house of the Harim clan). It is uncertain whether these are the same person.; [critical] The correct verse reference for Adna from the lineage of Pashhur is Ezra 10:39, not 10:30. In verse 39, "Shelemiah, Nathan and Adna" are mentioned among the sons of Pashhur.; [minor] The title is functional but could be improved to capture the dual role: both as a priest who divorced his foreign wife and as head of a priestly clan.; [minor] According to Ezra 10:22/39, Adna belonged to the lineage of Pashhur, and according to Neh 12:15, he was head of the Harim clan. versions.summary: Adna was a priest who lived in Judah in the period after the Babylonian exile, a time marked by religious and social restoration. In the book of Ezra, an Adna from the lineage of Pashhur is mentioned among the priests who had taken foreign wives and committed to sending them away as part of Ezra's extensive reform work (Ezra 10:30). In the book of Nehemiah, an Adna appears as head of the priestly house of the Harim clan during the days of high priest Joiakim (Neh 12:15). It is uncertain whether these two references concern the same person – the connection to different clans (Pashhur and Harim) may suggest that they are two different men with the same name. Regardless, both mentions testify to the central and complex role of the priesthood in rebuilding Jewish religious and community life after the exile.

footnotes.text: The name Adna (Hebrew: עַדְנָא) probably means "joy" or "delight" and is related to the Hebrew word 'eden' (עֵדֶן). The name form appears in several variants in the Old Testament, including Adnah (עַדְנָה), and testifies to a naming tradition connected with well-being and happiness.

The priestly family of Pashhur was one of the prominent priestly families after the exile. Pashhur son of Immer is known from the time of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 20:1–6), and the clan continued to play an important role in temple service after returning from Babylon. In Ezra 2:38, 1,247 descendants of Pashhur are mentioned among those who returned.

Ezra's reform against mixed marriages (around 458 BC) was one of the most far-reaching measures in the post-exilic period. The prohibition against marrying foreign women was primarily motivated by fear of religious syncretism—that foreign worship would infiltrate Israel's worship—not by ethnic purity as such. The background is found in Deuteronomy 7:1–4.

The question of whether Adna in Ezra 10 and Adna in Nehemiah 12:15 are the same person is debated. The timeframe makes it possible that they could be one person, but their association with different clans (Pashhur in Ezra, Harim in Nehemiah) suggests there may be two different people with the same name.

In rabbinic tradition, Ezra's reforms were seen as a continuation of the Torah's provisions regarding marital purity. The Talmud (Kiddushin 69b) discusses who is considered a legitimate Israelite after returning from exile, a topic that directly concerns those who had taken foreign wives.

Archaeological finds from the Persian period in Judea, including seals and bullae from Jerusalem and surrounding areas bearing priestly names and titles, confirm that the priestly families held prominent administrative roles in post-exilic society. Such findings align with the picture of priests like Adna holding leading positions within the temple institution.

The Harim clan was one of the significant priestly families in the post-exilic period. The clan is mentioned both among those who returned from exile (Ezra 2:39; Neh 7:42) and in the list of priestly houses with their heads during the time of Jehoiakim (Neh 12:15). That Adna served as head of this house shows that he held a prominent position in the temple organization.
